Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, LIG, 38000 Grenoble, France 2Department of Mathematics, University of Tübingen, 72076 Tübingen, Germany 3Department of Mathematics, University of California, Davis, CA 956168633, USA We present a modular algorithm for learning external potentials in continuousspace freefermion models including Coulomb potentials in any dimension. Compared to the latticebased approaches, the continuum presents new mathematical challenges: the state space is infinitedimensional and the Hamiltonian contains the Laplacian, which is unbounded in the continuum and thus produces an unbounded speed of information propagation. Our framework addresses these difficulties through novel optimization methods or informationpropagation bounds in combination with a priori regularity assumptions on the external potential. The resulting algorithm provides a unified and robust approach that covers both Coulomb interactions and other classes of physically relevant potentials. One possible application is the characterization of charge and position of nuclei and ions in quantum chemistry. Our results thus lay the foundation for a scalable and generalizable toolkit to explore fermionic systems governed by continuousspace interactions. I. INTRODUCTION Characterizing Hamiltonian evolution is essential for both the calibration and the deeper understanding of quantum devices and quantum mechanical systems. This task, often framed in the language of quantum information, is closely connected to classical inverse problems such as learning differential operators or reconstructing physical fields from observations, since it involves inferring the defining parameters of a Hamiltonian in a chosen representation from experimental data. Although Hamiltonian learning has been extensively studied in spin systems [1–6] and many more, where the local Hilbert space dimension is finite and the Hamiltonian is a bounded operator, much less is known about fermionic systems in continuous space. Unlike lattice models, these systems are naturally described by infinitedimensional state spaces and unbounded operators such as the Laplacian, which plays a central role in quantum theory. Physically, this setting is indispensable for modeling ions or molecules in free space, i.e., in the absence of a spatial lattice. To the best of our knowledge, no comparable continuous space fermionic learning model has yet been established, which is one motivation for the present work. Due to the enormous literature on Hamiltonian learning in the last years, we restrict ourselves to review a few works close to ours. Recent work on fermionic Hamiltonian learning treated lattice approximations [7], leaving open the challenge of handling the continuous space directly. In this work, the Hamiltonian Learning algorithm is implemented entirely in continuous space, which is the natural configuration space of particle positions ubiquitous, e.g., in quantum chemistry and the description of trapped quantum gases. Working in the continuum allows for natural representation of quantum states and dynamics, free from the discretization artifacts sometimes introduced by adhoc lattice models. E.g., continuous space preserves rotational and full translational symmetries and supports all plane wave solutions, which simplifies the analysis of free fermions and facilitate the extraction of physical parameters from experimental data. Furthermore, learning in continuous space avoids complications such as fermion doubling and latticeinduced boundary effects, making it particularly wellsuited for modeling systems where spatial resolution and smooth potential landscapes are essential. One potential application is the characterization of the charge number and position of ions in continuous space, ranging from a single test nucleus or ion to a Fermi gas approximation. Due to the ionic charge, the system is described by a Coulomb potential as follows: h = −∆+ V (1) with the external potential defined as: V (x) = K X k=1 λk ∥x −yk∥ where λj are the ion charges and yk ∈R3 are the nuclear positions. The learning task is to estimate both the parameters λk and the positions yk. This introduces a key distinction from previous work: the nonlinearity of the learning problem under consideration. Additionally, arXiv:2510.08471v1 [quantph] 9 Oct 2025 2 one encounters analytical challenges such as the regularity constraints imposed by the Laplacian as well as the Coulomb potential and the need to solve a highly nonlinear system to access the position of the Coulomb potential. Addressing these difficulties requires nonlinear numerical algorithms as well as a careful perturbation analysis of the Coulomb potential. Beyond the Coulomb case, we also consider broader classes of potentials, including smooth functions, hyperbolic functions, and polynomials. All of these models can be addressed within a unified data acquisition framework using our modularly designed algorithm. Here, parallelization exponentially reduces the sample complexity of the algorithm and allows for an efficient approximation of the considered potential. This requires novel informationpropagation bounds [12], as well as a careful choice of physical states to prepare due to the superselection rule. In detail, we first discuss the preliminaries and the protocol for acquiring the necessary data in Section II. Based on this data, we present a numerical algorithm for learning single and multiCoulomb potentials in Section III. Afterwards, the same data is used to learn any Lipschitz function or potentials that can be wellapproximated by polynomials or trigonometric functions, as shown in Section IV. Finally, detailed proofs and possible technical extensions are outlined in Section A–B. II. Then, the mutual influence on the output data is estimated and iteratively improved. In this way, the singleCoulomb case can be applied to the corrected and normalized data to find the positions and charge numbers up to a precision ε and with probability 1−δ.
